metadata.title: Grade 6 National High-Rigor Core Curriculum — 3-Week Integrated Unit
metadata.design_note: The United States does not have one federally mandated national sixth-grade curriculum. This plan is a high-rigor synthesis of influential nationwide frameworks and standards, emphasizing conceptual understanding, evidence, inquiry, problem solving, communication, creativity, and transfer.

national_frameworks.name: Common Core State Standards — Mathematics
national_frameworks.focus: Ratios and proportional relationships; rational numbers; expressions and equations; geometry; statistics and mathematical practices.

national_frameworks.name: Common Core State Standards — ELA/Literacy
national_frameworks.focus: Evidence-based reading, writing, speaking/listening, vocabulary, argumentation, and literacy across disciplines.

national_frameworks.name: Next Generation Science Standards
national_frameworks.focus: Three-dimensional science learning through practices, disciplinary core ideas, and crosscutting concepts.

national_frameworks.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies
national_frameworks.focus: Inquiry, disciplinary concepts, evaluating sources/evidence, communicating conclusions, and informed action.

national_frameworks.name: SHAPE America National Physical Education Standards
national_frameworks.focus: Motor competence, physical literacy, fitness, responsible behavior, and valuing physical activity.

metadata.essential_question: How can we use evidence, mathematics, science, history, and creative communication to understand systems and make responsible decisions?

learning_goals: Use ratios, rates, percentages, rational numbers, expressions, equations, geometry, and data to solve authentic problems.
Read complex informational and literary texts closely and support interpretations and claims with relevant evidence.
Explain scientific systems using models, data, cause-and-effect reasoning, and evidence.
Ask historical and civic questions, evaluate sources, distinguish evidence from claims, and communicate defensible conclusions.
Create, revise, present, and critique original artistic work.
Integrate knowledge across disciplines in a final evidence-based project.

weeks.title: Systems, Ratios, and Evidence
weeks.weekly_objective: Build a rigorous foundation in quantitative reasoning, close reading, scientific modeling, and source evaluation.

lessons.title: Thinking in Systems
objectives: Define a system and identify interacting parts.
Read an informational text and identify central ideas and supporting evidence.
Develop a question that can guide an investigation.
activities: Analyze a school, ecosystem, or community system.
Read a short informational passage and annotate claims, evidence, and key vocabulary.
Create a systems map showing components and relationships.
Write one investigable essential question.
lessons.assessment: Exit response: explain one system relationship and cite two pieces of evidence.
lessons.extension: Compare two systems and identify a shared pattern.

lessons.title: Ratios and Rates in the Real World
objectives: Represent equivalent ratios.
Calculate and interpret unit rates.
Explain quantitative reasoning in complete written sentences.
activities: Solve real-world scale, recipe, speed, and population-rate problems.
Represent ratios with tables, diagrams, and equations.
Write a short explanation defending one solution method.
lessons.assessment: Four-problem application set with one written justification.
lessons.extension: Create an original ratio problem with a verified solution.

lessons.title: Matter, Atoms, and Evidence of Change
objectives: Model matter at the atomic level.
Distinguish physical observations from interpretations.
Use evidence to determine whether a change may indicate a chemical reaction.
activities: Build particle models of simple substances.
Analyze before-and-after observations from a hypothetical reaction.
Organize observations in a data table.
Write a CER (claim-evidence-reasoning) response.
lessons.assessment: CER paragraph supported by at least two observations.

lessons.title: Sources, Claims, and Perspective
objectives: Distinguish primary and secondary sources.
Identify author, purpose, audience, and evidence.
Compare perspectives without confusing opinion with evidence.
activities: Evaluate two short sources describing the same historical event.
Complete a source-analysis matrix.
Identify corroborating and conflicting evidence.
Write a neutral synthesis.
lessons.assessment: Source-analysis paragraph with evidence from both sources.

lessons.title: Visualizing a System
objectives: Generate an original visual representation of a system.
Use composition and symbolism intentionally.
Explain artistic choices using discipline-specific vocabulary.
activities: Sketch a system diagram or infographic.
Use hierarchy, labels, scale, and visual emphasis.
Write an artist statement explaining three design choices.
lessons.assessment: Completed visual model plus artist statement.

questions.question: A ratio compares 12 red tiles to 18 blue tiles. What is the simplified ratio of red to blue?
What is the strongest evidence when evaluating a scientific claim?
questions.answer: Relevant observations or data that directly support the claim

questions.question: Which source is generally considered a primary source?
questions.answer: A diary written by a person who experienced the event

questions.question: What does a system model primarily show?
questions.answer: Parts of a system and relationships among them

questions.question: In a CER response, what connects evidence to the claim?

weeks.title: Change, Data, and Decision-Making
weeks.weekly_objective: Use rational numbers, equations, statistics, scientific evidence, and civic reasoning to analyze change and make defensible decisions.

lessons.title: Rational Numbers and Change
objectives: Compare and order positive and negative rational numbers.
Interpret quantities in context.
Use number lines and coordinate representations.
activities: Model temperature, elevation, financial balance, and ocean-depth changes.
Compare rational values using number lines.
Solve multi-step contextual problems.
lessons.assessment: Application set requiring interpretation of signed quantities.

lessons.title: Expressions and One-Variable Equations
objectives: Translate verbal relationships into expressions.
Solve one-variable equations.
Explain each algebraic step and verify solutions.
activities: Translate real-world relationships into equations.
Solve and check equations.
Write a brief explanation of why the solution is reasonable.
lessons.assessment: Six-equation mastery set with two contextual problems.

lessons.title: Statistics: Seeing Patterns in Data
objectives: Describe distributions using center and variability.
Identify patterns and possible outliers.
Use data to support or challenge a claim.
activities: Analyze a small environmental dataset.
Calculate mean and median.
Compare distributions visually.
Write a data-based conclusion.

lessons.title: Civic Decisions and Evidence
objectives: Identify a civic problem.
Evaluate evidence from multiple perspectives.
Develop a claim supported by evidence.
activities: Examine a fictional community resource-allocation problem.
Rank evidence by relevance and reliability.
Write and defend a recommendation.

lessons.title: Creative Communication: Data as Story
objectives: Transform quantitative information into an effective visual communication.
Select an appropriate chart or visual form.
Explain how design choices affect interpretation.
activities: Create an infographic using a provided dataset.
Add a concise explanatory paragraph.
Peer critique for accuracy, clarity, and visual hierarchy.

questions.question: Which measure is commonly used to describe the center of a dataset?
What makes evidence especially useful for a civic claim?
questions.answer: It is relevant, credible, and directly connected to the claim

questions.question: What is a primary purpose of an infographic?
questions.answer: To communicate information clearly through coordinated text and visuals

weeks.title: Integration, Argument, and Innovation
weeks.weekly_objective: Synthesize quantitative, scientific, historical, literary, and artistic evidence into an original solution and defend it.

lessons.title: Earth, Sun, Moon, and Cycles
objectives: Model relationships among Earth, Sun, and Moon.
Explain cyclic patterns such as lunar phases and seasons.
Use evidence and precise scientific language.
activities: Build or sketch an Earth-Sun-Moon model.
Sequence lunar phases.
Explain one cycle using a labeled model and paragraph.

lessons.title: Geometry of the Real World
objectives: Calculate area, surface area, and volume.
Apply geometry to a design problem.
Justify dimensions and material choices.
activities: Design a small community structure or exhibit.
Calculate required area and volume.
Produce a scaled sketch.

lessons.title: Argument: Claim, Evidence, and Counterclaim
objectives: Develop a clear claim.
Integrate evidence from multiple disciplines.
Address a reasonable counterclaim.
activities: Study a contested school/community design issue.
Build an evidence matrix.
Draft a structured argument with claim, evidence, reasoning, and counterclaim.

lessons.title: Innovation Studio
objectives: Synthesize information across disciplines.
Develop and revise a solution to a real-world problem.
Use feedback to improve the work.
activities: Select a problem involving resources, environment, learning, community, or design.
Research and document evidence.
Develop a quantitative component.
Create a visual or physical model.
Peer critique and revision.
lessons.assessment: Prototype, evidence portfolio, and revision log.

lessons.title: Presentation and Defense
objectives: Communicate a multidisciplinary conclusion clearly.
Defend choices using evidence.
Reflect on strengths, limitations, and next steps.
activities: Deliver a 5-7 minute presentation.
Present model, data, evidence, and argument.
Answer audience questions.
Complete a metacognitive reflection.

questions.question: Which model can be used to explain repeating patterns of lunar phases?
What information is needed to calculate the volume of a rectangular prism?
What is a counterclaim?
questions.answer: A reasonable opposing position that an argument addresses

questions.question: Why is revision important in an engineering or creative design process?
questions.answer: It uses feedback and evidence to improve the solution

questions.question: What makes a multidisciplinary conclusion strong?
questions.answer: It integrates relevant evidence and reasoning from more than one discipline

questions: Simplify and interpret a ratio in a real-world context.
Solve a multi-step problem involving rational numbers.
Solve and verify a one-variable equation.
Calculate area, surface area, or volume in a real-world design.
Interpret a statistical distribution and defend a conclusion.
Identify a central idea and cite supporting evidence.
Compare two perspectives using textual evidence.
Write a concise evidence-based argument.
Use precise domain vocabulary.
Deliver a structured oral explanation.
Use a model to explain a scientific system.
Analyze evidence of a physical or chemical change.
Explain conservation of matter in a chemical reaction.
Interpret data related to an Earth-Sun-Moon cycle.
Construct a claim supported by scientific evidence.
Evaluate a source for authorship, purpose, and evidence.
Distinguish primary and secondary sources.
Compare historical or civic perspectives.
Construct an evidence-based civic claim.
Explain how informed action can respond to a community problem.
Create or analyze a visual representation of a system.
Explain how artistic choices communicate meaning.
Connect an artistic work to personal, cultural, or historical context.
Revise work using criteria and feedback.
Reflect on how creative thinking contributed to problem solving.

performance_task.title: The Evidence-to-Action Challenge
performance_task.prompt: Choose a real or teacher-approved community, environmental, educational, or design problem. Define the problem, research credible evidence, analyze at least one dataset, apply at least two mathematical ideas, explain relevant scientific or social-system relationships, propose a solution, create a visual model or infographic, and defend the proposal in a 5-7 minute presentation.

assessment_philosophy.mastery_target: Recommended mastery threshold: 80% overall, with targeted reteaching when a student demonstrates a significant misconception.
assessment_philosophy.advanced_target: Students seeking honors-level challenge should justify methods, compare alternative strategies, evaluate limitations of evidence, and transfer concepts to unfamiliar contexts.
